2.text: traffic was carried on between the Reindeer Chukchee camps and the Maritime

3.text: villages (both Chukchee and Eskimo), and also between Asia and America

10.text: In the tale of “Elendi and his Sons,” the hero, coming to an American

11.text: Eskimo, requests “a score of ground-seal skins, a score each of bleached and

12.text: black-dyed coils of thong, the same of rough-seal skins; whatever you have,

13.text: one score of each.” The host asks for an equivalent, but Elendi has nothing:

14.text: so a quarrel arises, and they fight. Elendi vanquishes the Eskimo, commands

15.text: the people of the village to deliver up to him everything he had asked for,

16.text: and returns home carrying his subdued enemy away as a slave.¹

17.text: The chief part in such expeditions, however, belonged to the Nɵˊɵkalɪt

18.text: Eskimo of East Cape, although the Chukchee often accompanied them. It

19.text: is told that as late as three generations ago large parties would start from

20.text: East Cape for America. The Nɵˊɵkalɪt went in their large boats, sometimes

21.text: with thirty paddles in each; the Chukchee from the neighboring Arctic villages

22.text: went in smaller boats. These fleets crossed to America, carrying on trade

23.text: or piracy, as circumstances dictated. Similar expeditions of Eskimo and Chuk-

24.text: chee, though on a smaller scale, went over from Indian Point to St. Lawrence
